paragraphs.text: Dear elders and sisters, I hope you're enjoying the day and making the most of it. We understand from the Crosses, Nelsons, and Stoddards that the inspections went pretty well today. Making those apartments sparkle with cleanliness will make a big difference in making them less stressful to spend so much time in. When you're in a clean and well-organized space, it just feels a lot better.

Okay, so no new updates to share, but I do want to share a reminder about being wise with your time and use of the smartphones. Remember that agency allows you the ability to choose your own action, but it does not allow you to choose the consequence to your actions. The consequences are fixed and immutable, meaning they don't change no matter who you are or what your intentions might have been.

Natural law is, in a very real sense, law and it doesn't bend to personalities or charm or smooth talking or good intentions. Man's law can sometimes bend to these kinds of persuasions, but natural law never does. If an evil man walks off a ten-story building, he will fall to his death, and if an innocent child steps off a ten-story building, he or she will also fall to their death. So watch nature and reconcile yourself to it. In other words, face up to reality when it comes to agency and learn how to deal with it well. Don't think you can get freedom of choice and escape from consequences because it doesn't work that way in God's universe. It simply never has and it never will. So if you do face reality and acknowledge it, what happens is your capacity to overcome these challenges in reality grows. Ultimately, you are able to prevail and succeed in your mortal probation.

Now today, I'm going to share some thoughts about step three of the five-step process for achieving big and important goals which also simultaneously helps you to keep your focus on productive thoughts and actions and avoid wasting your time and energy on unproductive or inappropriate thoughts and actions. Step three is diagnose problems to get at their root causes. This step not only requires courage like step two, it also requires a commitment to logical analysis.

There are many people who try to get through life by simply following "their feelings." I think that some people inside the church even think that their feelings are somehow the same as a prompting from the Holy Ghost. This is simply not true. Our feelings are our feelings and they're not always accurate. In fact, many times they're not accurate. Promptings from the Holy Ghost are pure truth and we need to learn how to make a very strong distinction between our feelings and the promptings of the Holy Ghost which come in a sense as feelings. But there is a distinction between them and if you don't yet have a clear understanding of that, I'll give you a clue: always examine your motives. If your motive, the driving reason behind the decision you want to make is selfish or driven by some other un-Christ-like attribute, you can be sure that your feelings are not the same as the promptings of the Holy Ghost.

What we learn in Doctrine and Covenants Sections 8 and 9 is that the Lord expects us to use our minds to think things through carefully before he will confirm the truth to us. In verse 7, he says, "Behold, you have not understood; you have supposed that I would give it unto you when you took no thought save it was to ask me. But, behold, I say unto you, that you must study it out in your mind; then you must ask me if it be right."

So as we look at that, there's one more verse, verse 2, in section 8, that clearly spells out the order of priority. "Yea, behold, I will tell you in your mind and in your heart, by the Holy Ghost, which shall come upon you and which shall dwell in your heart." So what the Lord is, I think, trying to communicate to us is that he expects us to think about it, logically analyze the outcome, consider these feelings as they are consistent to, or not consistent to other revealed truth, and then we can trust our feelings after we've done our thinking. That's when he will come and confirm it to us, but he will confirm it to us in both our mind and our heart.

So in the process of diagnosis, we have to do some hard thinking. As I said before, hard thinking is hard and very few people want to do it. Don't be one of those kind of people. Don't be the kind of person who's unwilling to think hard about something. Being willing to think very, very hard about a problem allows you to produce answers that will be clear and understandable. If you want to really teach something in a simple, clear way so that even a child can understand, you have to think about it very carefully. You have to really tease out of it all of the little nuances so that you can then put it together in a way that someone else can understand it really easily.

The first phase of this step three is to focus on the "what is" before deciding what to do about it. Basically what this is speaking to is that so many people just jump right to a conclusion instead of thoroughly understanding what the situation really is, what the problem really is. It's a common mistake to move from identifying a tough problem to proposing a solution for it. Strategic thinking, however, requires both diagnosis and design.

A good diagnosis can take 15 minutes of thought up to an hour or two or three, depending on how well the thinking is and how complex the problem is. It involves speaking with other people sometimes and looking at the evidence to really determine the root causes. Like principles, root causes manifest themselves over and over and over again in different situations. In other words, one particular root cause can create a problem over here, another problem over there, a third problem over there, and a fourth problem over there. They're all coming from the same root cause. This is why principles are so important because principles get at the root causes. They don't sort of deal with all the symptoms out there. They're focusing in on the root causes and that's what you want to do too.

But to get at those root causes, you really have to deal with some hard thinking and this gets us into phase two of the step, which is to distinguish what are called proximate or close causes from root causes. A proximate cause or a close cause is typically something that leads to a problem. As an example, "I missed the bus because I didn't check the bus schedule." Yeah, that's true, but not checking the bus schedules is not actually the root cause. It's a proximate cause and it's a simple way to sort of solve the problem without solving the problem.

Root causes run much deeper and they're typically described with adjectives like this: "I didn't check the train schedule because I'm easily distracted and tend not to pay attention very well." Now you're getting at a root cause and once you're there, you can begin to deal with that weakness in you of being easily distracted and not paying attention. You've got a focus challenge. The fact that you didn't look at the schedule, well, that's true, but that wasn't the real problem. And when you get down into the deep, real root cause, you see that solving that cause or that root cause or that challenge or weakness in you is going to solve a whole bunch of other problems, not just missing the bus. So you can really only truly solve your problem by removing the root cause. And to do that, you have to distinguish between the symptoms and the actual disease itself.

The final phase is the hardest of all because it focuses on the human weaknesses that we all have. In order to properly diagnose the root causes, we have to, first of all, recognize that knowing what someone, including you, is like will tell you what you can expect from them. You're going to have to get over the reluctance that everybody seems to have when they get started in life of assessing people for what they really are instead of what you want them to be or what they say they are. The fact of the matter is you have to know the qualities of the people you surround yourself with. And that also goes for you. You can't be lying to yourself about who you really are because if you do, you'll never get down to solve the root causes that's stopping you from achieving the things that you want to achieve.

People almost always find it difficult to identify and accept their own mistakes and weaknesses. I do, you do, we all do. But it's a fact that we have to do it or else our blindness to our self will literally stop us from achieving anything worthwhile. Same thing with your associates, your friends, your colleagues. Most of them are pretty reluctant. They don't really want to point out your mistakes because they don't want to hurt your feelings or they don't want to have an awkward conversation. And I'm just telling you all need to get over this because more than anything else what differentiates people who live up to their potential from those who don't is their willingness to look at themselves and others objectively and understand the root causes standing in their way between where they are now and where they want to be.

The fundamental theme to step three is having what I call or is called intellectual honesty. You'll never find the true root cause to any problem that you're having if you're unwilling to be intellectually honest. That means you have to see yourself as you really are and see others as they really are. We've discussed this statement many times in the past, "you are what you do, not what you say you will do." We all struggle at times to walk our talk, but if we lie to ourselves about that when it happens then we are never going to solve it. We're going to have a very hard problem, probably an impossible problem, discovering root causes because we're not being honest about where we're breaking down, where we're failing.

You also have to be intellectually honest about others. You may have a friend who says all the right things but doesn't very often do the right things. If you're not intellectually honest about that you will begin to gather around you lots of friends that cannot be trusted to do what they say they're going to do. That kind of association will bend you and it will leave you unable to reach and achieve your goals. So until you can call yourself out on the areas where you fail and also call others out on the areas where they fail, you'll be constantly confused about why bad things keep happening to you.

However, once you become intellectually honest with yourself about yourself and others, then it will be very clear and simple about what the root causes are and how to design and plan to solve them. This design process will be our topic tomorrow and we'll get into that with some depth.

All right, elders and sisters, make it a great day. I love you and I'm growing in respect for you as you continue to show and grow your strengths in this interesting season we're in. Have a great day.
